:::{.definition data-title="Real Sequential Convergence"}

A real sequence $\{ x_{n} \}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ where for all $n \in N$, $x_{n} \in \mathbb{R}$ converges to some limit $x \in \mathbb{R}$ as $n\to \infty$ (denoted $x_{n } \to x$) when $$\forall \epsilon >0, \exists N\in \mathbb{N} :\forall n\geq N, |x_{n}-x|<\epsilon.$$

:::

**Proof Template**
- Let $\epsilon>0$ be arbitrary.
- Try to solve the inequality $|x_{n}-x|<\epsilon$ to determine how to choose
  $N \in \mathbb{N}$ so that this inequality holds for all $n \geq \mathbb{N}$.
- Show that the $N$ found actually works, namely for all $n \geq N$.

**Example**
To demonstrate how we use this result to show convergence we show that
$x_{n}=\frac{1}{n}$ converges to $0$ as $n \to \infty$. Fix $\epsilon>0$ and
find $N$ such that for all $n\geq N$
$$
\left| \frac{1}{n}\right|=\frac{1}{n}<\epsilon \implies N> \frac{1}{\epsilon }.
$$
